[Course context]
(Week 3) One attention head gives one view of the sentence; multiple heads give multiple views and can capture different relationships at the same time. Heads learn patterns; they are not manually assigned human meanings.

[Conversation so far]
(none)

[Student]
Why use multi-head attention instead of one head?

Read "The manager approved the access request after verifying the employee's role." How many different relationships can you spot, such as who approved and what was approved? Could one set of attention weights capture all of them at once?

[Course context]
(Week 5) Training loss shows whether learning is happening; validation loss shows whether learning generalises to unseen text. Very low training loss with rising validation loss may indicate overfitting.

[Conversation so far]
Student: How do I know if my model is learning well?

[Student]
If training loss is very low, the model is great.
Low training loss tells you the model fits the data it learned from. Which other loss tells you about text it has never seen? If training loss keeps falling while that one rises, what is happening?

[Course context]
(Week 5) Unlabelled text creates its own labels: shift the text by one token and the next token becomes the target. No human labels are required, which is why pretraining can use huge text collections.

[Conversation so far]
Student: How can you train on unlabelled text if there are no labels?
Tutor: Take "The user clicked the phishing link." Hide the last word: did a human need to write the correct answer? What happens if you apply the same trick to every position in a huge pile of text?

[Student]
So the next word is the label, and the text labels itself.

That's it. Shifting the text by one token gives every position a free target, which is why pretraining can use huge text collections. Compare with Week 6: why does spam classification need labelled data when pretraining doesn't?

[Course context]
(Week 6) For classification, a linear classification head replaces next-token scoring and produces one score per class, e.g. two logits for spam and not spam. The final token representation is commonly used because it has attended to the previous tokens.

[Conversation so far]
(none)

[Student]
Just tell me what a classification head is.

Here's the starting point: it's a small layer added on top of the pretrained model. Spam detection has only two possible outputs, so instead of a score for every vocabulary word, how many scores should this layer produce?
